![](images/aa/aa730804a15decac8450255e714ca1e0697f4f2326eb615d4d035a2870a49dce.png)

Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_D \dfrac{2y}{x^2+y^2} \: \textrm{d}A,$ where the region $D$ is shown above.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\dfrac{1}{2}$ centered at $\left(0,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\!.$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For $x^2+\left( y-\dfrac{1}{2} \right)^2=\dfrac14,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r = \sin\theta.$

- For $y=\dfrac{1}{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{2} \\ r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{2} \\ r & =\frac{1}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ r & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta.$ Our curves intersect at the point $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{1}{2}\right).$ So, the entire region lies between the radial lines $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2},$ as depicted below.  

![](images/12/1284a8b4b3f1634b4f7586d40ab8adf9cf93c69484b7ed069f138c8055e88892.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$ as 

$$
\Delta = \Big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: \dfrac{1}{2}\csc\theta \leq r \leq \sin\theta, \: \dfrac{\pi}{4} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2} \Big\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1/2\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{1/2\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta [r]_{1/2\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )]_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(0-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}\frac{1}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}A,$ where the region $D$ is enclosed between two circles centered at $O$ of radii $2$ and $3,$ as shown above.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents the annulus between the disks of radii $2$ and $3$ centered at the origin. 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ we obtain $r=2.$

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9,$ we obtain $r=3.$

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,2\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{{r}^{4}}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{{r}^{3}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[-\frac{1}{2{r}^{2}}]}_{2}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\frac{1}{8}-\frac{1}{18})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{5}{72}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{5}{72}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{5}{72}\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{36}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16,$ we obtain $r=4.$

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=36,$ we obtain $r=6.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{x{y}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{4}^{6}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\int }_{4}^{6}\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {[r]}_{4}^{6}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (6-4)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{[\frac{{sin}^{3}⁡\theta }{3}]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =0.\end{aligned}

![](images/da/da18aafec278b5d44b0530097729e4cb4b319e219c005fc155d78fab8aa90937.png)

![](images/ce/ce35f6ef14576f536c268dd7420af6e0226609ab5305e85770f400439c2435de.png)

Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A,$ where the region $D$ is shown above.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\frac{1}{2}$ centered at $(\frac{1}{2},0)\,.$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2}=\frac{1}{4},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{4}+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

- For $x=\frac{1}{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2} \\ r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{2} \\ r & =\frac{1}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\ r & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the point $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$  So, the entire region lies between the radial lines $\theta =0$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{4},$ as depicted below.  

![](images/f5/f518a206638071a7b8548882a453123b6d78aed0aa94cc0e6e23429f22c6f1b3.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \le r\le \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta /2}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\int }_{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta /2}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta [r]_{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta /2}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$

$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ we obtain $r=2.$

- For $y=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-1 \\ r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =-1 \\ r & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ r & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the point $(\sqrt{3},-1).$ So, the entire region lies between the radial lines $\theta =-\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $\theta =-\frac{\pi }{6},$ as depicted below.  

![](images/23/2386c1dcb1cf71231f2bb508dc1dd85dadef15b806eaf7f9a9ad0d3e4f3da1ca.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \le r\le 2,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le -\frac{\pi }{6}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /6}{\int }_{-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /6}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /6}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta [r]_{-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /6}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (2+\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /6}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\theta ]_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /6} \\  & =[(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{6})-\frac{\pi }{3})-(0-\pi )] \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}-2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{6x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{6r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{4}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\int }_{2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta [r]_{2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (4-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(24\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -12\sqrt{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[24\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -12\sqrt{2}\,\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =[(24\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-12\sqrt{2}(\frac{\pi }{4}))-0] \\  & =12\sqrt{2}-3\pi \sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
![](images/bf/bf7089294bc72330065590a9fe54acebee6d0ab982bffb4a162407c7232898ec.png)

Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}\frac{4y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A,$ where the region $D$ is shown above.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at $(0,1).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y-1)^{2} & =1 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)^{2} & =1 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1 & =1 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

- For $y=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =1 \\ r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ r & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ r & =\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the point $(-1,1).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{4},$ as depicted below.  

![](images/1b/1b83e2674bba4bd6c326083f8c94496b5288de23575dc63a92b9a660eba69f67.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \le r\le 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{4}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{4y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{4r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}{\int }_{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta [r]_{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-4{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-2[\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )]_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4} \\  & =-2[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )] \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A,$ where the region $D$ is enclosed between two circles centered at $O$ of radii $1$ and $3,$ as shown above.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents the annulus between the disks of radii $1$ and $3$ centered at the origin. 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ we obtain $r=1.$

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9,$ we obtain $r=3.$

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}\sqrt{{r}^{2}}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}]}_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(9-\frac{1}{3})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{26}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{26}{3}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{26}{3}\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =\frac{52\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin.

$$

- For $x=1,$ we get

$$

$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the point $(1,\sqrt{3}).$ So, the entire region lies between the radial lines $\theta =0$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3},$ as depicted below.  

![](images/10/1060c071df1dbd197c14da529819a34bd4457868fdd4cbe78a7f93f12dbf67da.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{4x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{2}4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\int }_{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta [r]_{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (2-\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}(8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -4)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -4\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =[(8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\frac{4\pi }{3})-0] \\  & =4\sqrt{3}-\frac{4\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
